narrative: The model estimated a 12% probability that you will fail your final year. That is a low risk rather than a forecast of certain failure, but in this process it is enough for you to be required to take remedial courses as a precaution. The three strongest influences on the prediction were your weekly study time, your history of past class failures, and your reason for choosing the school. Importantly, all three leaned toward passing rather than failing: your 5–10 hours of weekly study is more than the most common 2–5 hours among students who passed; having no past failures matches the passing average; and choosing the school for home-related reasons was treated as a lower-risk signal. The model therefore did not find strong evidence that you are likely to fail. The remedial requirement reflects the remaining, smaller risk that still needs to be managed. To improve your position, protect the habits already helping you: keep a steady study routine, maintain attendance, and avoid accumulating failures. Since you are not currently receiving school or family educational support, consider asking what help is available and use the remedial courses to target any weak areas. Your wish to continue to higher education is also a strong reason to keep focused.
